phrases.text: Every minute you work in HBCField is measured by two clocks.
The first is your shift. It starts when you clock in, and stops when you clock out. That is your working day.
The second is job time: the minutes you spend on one job.
And one rule sits under everything else in this video.
Job time only ever counts inside your shift. Never before you clock in. Never after you clock out.
You clock in on your phone when you arrive.
At a site with an address, the phone checks that you are really there. Working away from a site is possible only where your workspace allows it.
During the day you take your rests. A rest is cut out of your time, and out of any job you are on.
When the day is done, you clock out. From clock in to clock out, minus the rests: that is your shift.
A job can only start when the person doing it is clocked in. In the office, out on the road, on the phone and on the web.
If you tap a step that starts work, and you are not clocked in, the app does not just refuse.
It offers one button: clock in, and start work. One tap does both.
And if your phone dies on site, the office can start the job for you. But only with a reason, and never before your clock in.
The job's history then says exactly who did it, for whom, and why. And you get a message.
A job moves through steps, and each step counts as a different kind of time.
Accepting a job, the evening before, counts nothing.
From On the way until you arrive is travel.
From Start work until Complete is working time. That is the number people mean when they ask how long a job took.
If something stops you, you report an issue. From that moment until you resume, the time is blocked. It is kept apart, so a missing part never looks like slow work.
None of this needs a timer running. Every tap is saved with its own time, even without signal, and the times are worked out from those moments.
Two more rules keep the numbers honest.
First: job time only counts while you are clocked in, and your rests are taken out.
Second: you can only be on one job at a time. If two of your jobs are open at once, each minute goes to the job you moved last.
So the hours on your jobs can never add up to more than the hours on your timesheet. What a client is billed, and what you worked, come from the same moments.
So what happens when your shift ends, and the job is not finished?
When you clock out, the app shows the jobs you are still working on. For each one, you can finish it, or leave a handover note: what you did, and what is left.
Either way, the job pauses at the exact minute you clock out. Nothing counts overnight.
And clocking out is never blocked. If your phone is dead, or the shift is closed for you, the job still pauses. It is simply marked: no handover yet.
If you did not write a note, the app asks you every time you open it, until you do. It never stops you from clocking in.
Once you are clocked in, the paused job is right there. Resume work, and your time starts counting again from that tap.
Now let's follow one big job, from start to finish. A boiler room replacement at Pilgrove Hotels. It takes ten working days.
Days one to four belong to Tobias.
On day one he clocks in, taps On the way, and arrives thirty minutes later. That half hour is the job's only travel.
Every morning after that he clocks in, drives to the hotel, and taps Resume work on site. The drive is on his shift, but not on the job.
His lunch is taken out. At half past three he clocks out, and the job pauses until the next morning.
On day three, a pump part is missing. Tobias reports an issue. One hour and twenty minutes are blocked, until the part arrives and he resumes.
On day four, his phone dies before he clocks out. The shift is closed for him, the job pauses, and it is marked: no handover yet.
Day five. Tobias is off sick, and Mara, in the office, gives the job to Priya.
Before she does, she is warned. Tobias has not written a handover yet, and he has worked twenty-eight hours and twenty minutes on this job.
She can wait for his note, or reassign anyway, and leave Priya a note of her own.
Later that morning, Tobias writes his handover from home. Priya gets it straight away. It sits at the top of the job: what was done, what is left, and his time.
Priya's own time starts when she taps Start work. Tobias's hours stay his. Priya's start from zero.
Priya works the job for the rest of that week and the next, and on day ten, at twenty-five to one, she completes it.
Here is what the system knows.
Tobias: twenty-eight hours and twenty minutes of work, half an hour of travel, and one hour twenty blocked.
Priya: forty hours and twenty-five minutes of work.
The whole job: sixty-eight hours and forty-five minutes of work, over ten working days.
The weekend, the nights, the lunch breaks, the morning drives and the day the job sat paused: none of it counted as job time.
You will find all of this on the job itself, and in Reports, Job time: every job a person worked on, with travel, working and blocked time, right beside their time on the clock.
So, six rules.
One: clock in to start work.
Two: travel, working and blocked are kept apart.
Three: time only counts inside your shift, with rests taken out.
Four: one job at a time.
Five: clocking out pauses the job.
And six: whoever takes a job over starts from zero.
That is time in HBCField.
